item.title: Scotland keen to bounce back against 'wounded' Australia
item.description: Both Scotland and Australia are capable of scintillating highs and crushing lows, but who will come out on top at Murrayfield on Sunday?
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Two sides who are thrilling and perplexing in almost equal measure, Scotland versus Australia in the Nations Championship on Sunday could be described as the Battle of the Unpredictables.

These are two teams that when they are hot, they are very hot, but both have the capacity to fall so far below their ceiling they are left staring up at it from the floor.

Both are coming off chastening defeats last weekend - the Wallabies taken apart by England at Twickenham, and Scotland taken to the cleaners by New Zealand at Murrayfield.

This is a fixture that stokes the fires of Scotland's Australia-born captain Sione Tuipulotu, but making amends for that second-half no-show against the All Blacks is providing the primary motivation.

"It is always hard to watch the footage back after a defeat like that where we missed some big opportunities and let ourselves down in certain areas," Tuipulotu said.

"As a group, we have confronted that and I've been very proud of the boys in terms of how they have rallied this week.

"We know that Australia will also be a wounded team coming here after what happened against England at Twickenham.

"I think I will always have that little bit of fire bubbling away whenever I play against the Wallabies.

"I've done it a few times now, both with Scotland and also with the Lions. But there's a bigger picture than just looking at me and my history with Australia.

"Our minds are firmly set on bouncing back after last week. That performance wasn't good enough. We know that and we want to put that right."

Tuipulotu wary of Suaalii response

In the wake of the Wallabies' humbling at Twickenham, much of the criticism was aimed at Joseph Suaalii. Much like with Finn Russell and Scotland, Suaalii is the superstar that, more than any other player, carries the hopes of his nation.

When things go wrong, as they did against England, the 23-year-old rugby league convert tends to be the first in the firing line.

"This Suaalii gamble, I dread to think how much he gets paid. He doesn't look like an international rugby union player to me," said the former England international Chris Ashton, who himself made the switch from league to union.

Having started on the wing at Twickenham last weekend, Suaalii reverts to the 13 jersey at Murrayfield, throwing him back into the midfield maelstrom against Tuipulotu.

The pair had a memorable collision when the sides met two years ago, Suaalii nailing Tuipulotu with a shuddering hit of such force that the man dishing out the crunching tackle was himself invalided out of the game.

The words exchanged between the players in the aftermath were spicy as Suaalii left the pitch, but Tuipilotu has a huge respect for the threat he poses on Sunday, and thinks the flak flying his way will serve only to light a fire to ram the critics' words back down their throats.

"I know there's been a few things flying around this week about him. I wish they could have done that in another week," Tuipulotu joked.

"My brother [Mosese, now with Edinburgh] was with him at the Waratahs and he only had good things to say about him to be honest.

"I know how much of a talented athlete he is and there's only so much you can poke someone before they respond.

"We are wary of the bounce back and we're certainly not delusional enough to think that these kind of players won't play well against us.

"I expect the very best version of Joseph Suaalii in this game and I'm excited to go up against him again."

France's epic victory over world champions South Africa in Paris on Friday all but ended Scottish hopes of finishing first in the northern hemisphere table.

All they can do now is deliver wins over Australia and then Japan next week to ensure they have a meaningful game against one of the southern hemisphere heavyweights on finals weekend in London.

Some precious top-level action in the bank ahead of next year's World Cup would be vital. A dead-rubber against a middling opponent, not so much.

"For us, it's a got-to-have-it game," said Tuipulotu. "That's the mood in the camp. It's such a different feeling around the place when you've either won or lost.

"We know we need to win this game. We want to get that positive feeling back around the camp again.

"We want to get our Nations Championship back on track again and give ourselves a big game going into that finals weekend."

item.title: McIlroy fades as Hatton leads in Dubai
item.description: Rory McIlroy's hopes of an eighth Race to Dubai title are dented as Tyrrell Hatton takes the outright lead into the fourth round of the DP World Tour Championship.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

DP World Tour Championship third-round leaderboard

-9 T Hatton (Eng); -8 V Perez (Fra); -6 M Lindberg (Swe); -5 A Scott (Aus), E Chacarra (Spa), F Laporta (Ita), R McIlroy (NI)

Selected others: -4 D Bradbury (Eng), J Schaper (SA), K Reitan (Nor); -3 M Wallace (Eng), J Dean (Eng), J Rahm (Spa); +3 P Reed (US), T Fleetwood (Eng)

Rory McIlroy's hopes of winning a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title faded as he fell four shots behind leader Tyrrell Hatton after three rounds of the season-ending DP World Tour Championship.

Northern Irishman McIlroy started Saturday tied for the lead with Hatton but, while the Englishman remained at the top of the field with a four-under-par 68, McIlroy fell away with a 72 at the Earth Course in Dubai.

Hatton, on nine under for the tournament, holds a one-shot lead over France's Victor Perez as he bids for a first DP World Tour Championship, while Sweden's Mikael Lindberg is third on six under.

McIlroy is joint fourth in a group of four players which includes Spain's Eugenio Chacarra, the current leader in the Race to Dubai standings.

Six-time major champion McIlroy began the tournament trailing Chacarra by more than 500 points, but knowing a win would guarantee him an eighth season-long crown to equal the tally set by Scotland's Colin Montgomerie.

McIlroy will clinch the title if he finishes ahead of Chacarra and in the top four.

McIlroy took the outright lead with an eagle three on the par-five seventh, before bogeys on the eighth, ninth and 10th.

A birdie on the 14th was followed by another dropped shot on the 15th, but McIlroy finished with a birdie at the par-five 18th after narrowly missing a six-foot eagle putt.

Hatton scrambled a par at the last after driving into the water and finding a greenside bunker with his approach shot.

He will play alongside Perez, who carded a 67, on the final day.

"It would mean a lot to go on and win tomorrow," said Hatton.

"There is a lot that can change. The course is playing difficult this week and there's a lot of fantastic players just behind. It is going to be a tough day."

Spain's Jon Rahm, who could clinch the Race to Dubai title with victory on Sunday, fell six shots off the lead with a third consecutive 71.

Chacarra, four shots adrift off the lead after two rounds, carded a 68 that included nine birdies, three bogeys and a double bogey.

McIlroy will play alongside Englishman Dan Bradbury, who climbed to four under with a stunning 66.

Chacarra, four shots adrift off the lead after two rounds, carded a 68 that included nine birdies, three bogeys and a double bogey.

Lindberg will play in the penultimate group alongside Australia's 2013 Masters winner Adam Scott, who went round a 67.

Follow live text updates on the DP World Tour Championship final round on the BBC Sport website and app on Sunday.

item.title: Taylor-Brown wins in Dubai to top T100 standings
item.description: British triathlete Georgia Taylor-Brown moves top of the overall standings in the women's T100 series with her second victory of the season in Dubai.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

British triathlete Georgia Taylor-Brown held on to win the penultimate race of the women's T100 season in Dubai and move top of the overall standings.

The 2020 Olympic silver medallist claimed her second victory of the season in the fourth event of the campaign, with December's grand final in Qatar remaining.

Taylor-Brown will take a six-point advantage over Switzerland's Julie Derron into that final event.

The 32-year-old Mancunian, who is a former world champion in the shorter Olympic distance and finished third in this season's World Triathlon Series, is aiming for her first T100 world title.

Taylor-Brown won her first T100 race - which includes a 2km swim, 80km bike ride and 18km run - in Spain in May and was third in Vancouver, Canada in August.

She hit the front in Dubai just under 4km into the run and opened a 30-second advantage before holding off New Zealand's Nicole van der Kaay to win by just 10 seconds, finishing in three hours 35 minutes and 19 seconds.

Derron, who took the lead in the overall standings with victory in Vancouver, was third in Dubai, finishing two minutes seven seconds behind Taylor-Brown.

Britain's Kate Waugh, the 2025 champion, was ninth, just ahead of team-mate Lizzie Rayner.

Waugh missed the opening two events of the season with a calf injury and is eighth overall heading into next month's Grand Final in Doha.

item.title: 'Exciting' Moylan flourishing for club and country
item.description: BBC Sport NI looks as Jack Moylan's terrific form for Cardiff City and Republic of Ireland ahead of the Irish's final two Nations League games.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Jack Moylan made his intent clear when speaking to the media in August soon after joining Cardiff City in the summer from Lincoln City.

He outlined how he wanted to impress for the Welsh club and ensure he was a mainstay in Republic of Ireland squads after winning his first two caps in May.

Fast forward three months and the 25-year-old has certainly come good on those promises by stepping up for club and country.

Under fellow Irish man Brian Barry-Murphy at Cardiff he has netted 11 goals in 17 games in all competitions while also providing three assists.

On the international stage, Moylan featured in all four of Republic of Ireland's Nations League games in the extended September/October window, scoring and assisting in a 3-0 win against Israel.

Already a key player for the Bluebirds, Moylan is emerging as an important attacking threat for his country too and will be pivotal in their final two Nations League games against Austria and Kosovo.

It is the latest chapter in the rapid rise of Moylan, who has gone from strength to strength since earning a move to Lincoln in January 2024.

Moylan 'comfortable from the first minute' at international level

Moylan joined the Imps from Irish Premier Division side Shelbourne after a stellar final season with the Dublin club in which he finished as the league's joint highest scorer with 15 goals.

At the time of the move, he said it was "the next step" in his career and, after an initial bedding in period and two separate spells on the treatment table with an ankle problem, his and Lincoln's form exploded from November 2025 onwards.

The versatile attacker scored 11 goals and provided six assists last season as Lincoln won promotion and beat Cardiff to the League One title.

His impressive campaign led to a first call-up to the Irish senior squad in May and he marked his debut with a hat-trick in a 5-0 win against Grenada before he was sent off in his second game as they drew with Qatar.

Cardiff came calling in the summer and Moylan made the move to Wales on a four-year deal for an undisclosed fee.

He scored the winner on his debut in the EFL Cup against Swindon and three more followed before the first international break, but he has really kicked on since returning to club duty in early October, proving he has adapted to life in the Championship seamlessly.

Moylan, who has featured as a false nine, a number 10 and off the left this season, has seven goals in his last seven league games, including a first-half hat-trick against West Ham with his first goal a fine finish from outside the box.

His boss at club level told BBC Sport Wales in October that Moylan is a "very exciting player to watch because of how attack-minded he is".

Republic of Ireland fans were treated to snippets of those attacking talents in the first four Nations League games.

After coming off the bench in the defeat against Kosovo, Moylan started the next three games, coming in off the right to link well with Troy Parrott and Adam Idah.

He impressed alongside those two players in the comprehensive win over Israel, setting up Idah's goal before racing through and calmly slotting home.

He was a livewire in the draws that followed against Austria and Israel and is in the frame to continue his burgeoning relationship with star striker Parrott, starting with Saturday's trip to Linz to face Austria.

His international boss Heimir Hallgrimsson knew that he had unearthed a gem from the moment Moylan arrived to train with the senior squad for the first time and hopes there is plenty more to come from him in a green shirt.

"Moylan of course has taken the headlines and taken the spotlight the last couple of weeks and hopefully he can transfer that into the national team," he said.

"His rise has been really fast, but that's brilliant when you find someone in the May [friendly] camp, coming in and scoring three goals in his first game and since then he's been involved in the starting 11 more or less.

"Absolute impact from his first game. Sometimes you need up to 10 games to be comfortable at this level, but he was comfortable from the first minute and from the first training session he had a 'wow' impact."

While it is early days with club and his country, the signs are good that Moylan's trajectory is set to continue on the upward curve it has been trending at over the last two years.

item.title: NI target challenge of Nations League promotion
item.description: A win against Ukraine on Saturday night would leave Northern Ireland needing only a point away to Hungary next week to secure promotion to Nations League A for the first time.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Before this Nations League campaign, Northern Ireland had won just one of 16 games played in the second tier of the competition.

But after eight points from four games across September and October, all without conceding a goal, Michael O'Neill's side could end Saturday night as a League A side for the first time.

For that to come to pass, Hungary would need to lose to Georgia in Tbilisi [17:00 GMT] before a Northern Ireland win at home to Ukraine in the later kick-off.

Even if only they hold up their end of the bargain with a win at Windsor Park, the side would travel to Budapest on Tuesday night knowing a point would be good enough to top the group and seal promotion.

"You do look at the teams that do step up and it's tough. We've seen teams do that before and they find it very difficult," said O'Neill after stressing his side would be looking no further than the first game of this double-header.

"But for us to get that opportunity to play against those big teams in a competitive group stage would be great, it would be great for the development of the team.

"I wouldn't say the results at that point wouldn't be important, but I think we'd learn a lot."

Northern Ireland v Ukraine

Uefa Nations League

Saturday, 14 November at 19:45 GMT

Watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two NI from19:15 GMT; Listen on BBC Sounds and BBC Radio Ulster; Watch, listen, live text and clips on BBC Sport app & website

Strong performance in the Nations League carries multiple rewards.

Finishing in the top two of their group - something Northern Ireland would confirm with a draw against Ukraine - would ensure O'Neill's side are among the second group of seeds when the draw for Euro 2028 qualifying is made in Belfast next month.

There is also the potential backdoor route into the qualification play-offs too, the same method used by Northern Ireland to find themselves just two games from the summer's World Cup despite finishing third in their group.

But for O'Neill promotion would also bring the less tangible benefit of showing his squad what is required to reach the very top.

O'Neill has previously sought out friendlies against the likes of Spain and France, drawing praise from his then Les Bleus counterpart Didier Deschamps for taking a game against the latter on the eve of the World Cup when others had not been so keen.

Midfielder Shea Charles previously spoke of how going up against the likes of Spain's Rodri in such fixtures helped "prepare" him for the Premier League before he got his £30m move to Fulham.

And O'Neill feels further exposure to such challenges, especially in regular competitive fixtures, would be hugely beneficial to others in his largely inexperienced side.

He added: "That's good for any player, but particularly young players, because it lets them see what's required, what's required to be a Spanish international and playing in the Champions League or playing your club football at the highest level in Europe.

"We want our players to aspire to try to get there too."

Barnsley midfielder Patrick Kelly scored his first international goal in that game against France, the strike coming on a night he shared the field with the likes of Kylian Mbappe, Ousmane Dembele and Michael Olise.

The 22-year-old, who joined the Tykes in the summer of 2025 having not made a senior appearance for West Ham, has played all his club football in either League One, League Two, or the Irish Premiership.

"Playing those bigger nations, it would only improve us as a team," he said.

"You want to test yourself against the best. A couple of the lads have experienced it, they would have played Germany in the last [qualifying ]campaign and done well, and I had it that night against France.

"Playing against the best players in the world, you see where you're at and the team as well."

Having missed that game against France through suspension, Blackburn Rovers defender Tom Atcheson's only international start coming into this campaign had been against Guinea, but the 20-year-old senses the team is ready for the step up.

"I think we do belong there and we're showing it," he said. "We want to have those challenges, we want to challenge ourselves against the best because it's exciting times.

"We know what we're capable of. To get into League A with those massive nations would be unbelievable, that's where we all want to get.

"We're looking forward to the next two games and hopefully to make that happen."

item.title: Sooryavanshi becomes youngest captain in men's T20s
item.description: Teenage India sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi breaks the record held by Croatia's Zach Vukusic as the youngest captain in top-level men's Twenty20 cricket.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has become the youngest captain in top-level men's Twenty20 cricket after taking charge of his state side Bihar on Saturday.

Captaining at the age of 15 years and 232 days, Sooryavanshi broke the record held by Zach Vukusic, who captained Croatia aged 17 years and 311 days.

Bihar lost their opening match in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy - India's domestic state T20 competition, below the Indian Premier League (IPL) - by five wickets to Saurashtra, with Sooryavanshi making 18 from 12 balls.

It is the latest landmark the young career of Sooryavanshi, who became India's youngest men's international in July when he made his T20 debut against England.

He has broken numerous records since making his IPL debut for Rajasthan Royals as a 14-year-old in 2025, becoming the franchise tournament's youngest player.

He became the youngest centurion in men's T20s when hitting a hundred against Gujarat Titans later that season, and this year was the tournament's leading run-scorer.

Sooryavanshi played in two of India's five T20 internationals in New Zealand earlier this month, with a top score of 45 in the third match in Wellington.

He is also due to be part of India's side at the Rising Stars Asia Cup, a development 50-over tournament which takes place in Doha later this month.

item.title: Menzies sheds weight & embraces fitness after health issues
item.description: Cameron Menzies has lost five stone and embraced fitness and different forms of therapy after medical issues threatened to upend his darts careers.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Cameron Menzies has lost five stone after hand surgery and a medical fright threatened to upend his darts career.

The Scot, 37, needed an operation for an injury sustained repeatedly punching a drinks table on stage following his first-round exit at the PDC World Championships last December.

And he made headlines during the summer after requiring medical attention during his World Matchplay encounter with Ross Smith, which he had to forfeit.

His dizzy turn was put down to high blood pressure caused by dehydration.

"I didn't know what it was, I looked at the board and I just felt like everything was spinning," Menzies told BBC Scotland.

"They took me off the stage, there were paramedics and first aid on site and they were taking my blood pressure and it was up to over 200, and they were going to phone an ambulance because that was like heart attack material.

"But as soon as they gave me a drink of water it dropped massively. They wouldn't let me leave the venue until they were quite happy with it and then when I came back up to Glasgow the next day I went to the Royal Infirmary and got bloods taken and stuff – it was just high blood pressure dehydration.

"I have got a little blood pressure machine now. I have been taking that as much as possible and everything has been fine.

"I just make sure I drink a lot more water. It was warm that day, I had a lot of TV stuff to do and I maybe didn't look after myself much because it had never happened before and hopefully never happens again."

On his weight loss, Menzies elaborated: "My heaviest was 21-and-a-half stone, I didn't realise how big I was until I see pictures now and I am like, 'wow I was big'.

"It was for my health to try and lose weight because I had a thing last year with my heart so I went to the hospital and found out that I have got an ectopic heartbeat so my heart skips an extra beat.

"They told me to try and lose weight before they did anything with tablets, so thankfully it has dropped to a level where it is fine, I don't need tablets.

"I just usually do a 5k, I don't do many weights because then I can't throw darts but I just go for a jog. It is good for my physical health and it is good for my mental health, I never leave the gym feeling bad, I like doing it for that as well."

It is not just Menzies who has got the fitness bug, with a host of other top players seeing the benefits of being in good shape.

"You look at the players nowadays, most of them are starting to look after themselves now," Menzies added.

"Luke Humphries lost a power of weight, there have been a few more.

"Most of the hotels we stay in have got gyms and a lot of guys are just popping to the gym or they go on 5k runs. Even the commentators and the referees are doing it.

"The darts world is changing, I do think in the future you will get a lot more people looking like sportsmen rather than darts players."

How sports psychology & hypnotherapy have helped

Eleven months on from his hand injury, Menzies appears to have made a full recovery and has gone on to enjoy a solid season, winning two PDC ProTour titles this year.

He is preparing to compete at the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton this weekend, but feared he might never return to top level darts.

"At the start of the year I thought that could have been me because I had no feeling in my hands after the operation," he said.

"I was in a bandage for six weeks, and the first three or four months I couldn't feel a dart, so I am lucky.

"Obviously it was my own fault but I am lucky enough that I can still play at a good level.

"With the [Luke] Littler effect the prize money is good. I had a good job before as a plumber but the money in darts these days is life changing."

Up until relatively recently, the Ayrshire player often struggled to control his emotions on the oche, which clearly inhibited his undoubted talent.

The world number 26 has a calmer demeanour now - something that has been helped by his decision to embrace sports psychology and hypnotherapy.

"Every night I have got a track to listen to. The sport psychologist does the hypnotherapy treatment and at night you listen to him talking to you. He is just talking to your subconscious, the same thing every night when you go to sleep.

"I usually fall to sleep after 15 minutes - it is just talking to your brain really rather than yourself.

"I feel like it has helped."

item.title: Tuchel to remind England of anti-racism protocols before Spain game
item.description: Manager Thomas Tuchel will remind England's players of Uefa's anti-racism protocols before Sunday's Nations League fixture against Spain in Madrid.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Manager Thomas Tuchel will remind England's players of Uefa's anti-racism protocols before Sunday's Nations League fixture against Spain in Madrid.

The match will be England's first in the Spanish capital since a notorious fixture at Real Madrid's Bernabeu stadium in 2004 which was overshadowed by racist chanting aimed at England players.

The Spanish federation was fined last month and ordered to play their next friendly match with a partial stadium closure after fans sang "Islamophobic and xenophobic" chants about Muslims during a game against Egypt.

"We had a same discussion before the Serbia game [in Belgrade in September 2025]," Tuchel said. "There is a protocol in place.

"Maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid]."

European governing body Uefa, the organiser of the Nations League, has a three-step protocol to handle incidents of discrimination inside stadiums, designed to give referees the power to halt matches, and even abandon games if racist behaviour continues.

In the first instance, referees halt the match and request an announcement on the public address system.

Then, if discrimination continues, officials can stop the game for five to 10 minutes and take the players from the field.

If issues continue after the second stoppage, then the game can be abandoned.

"It's important that the players know about the protocol," Tuchel said.

"And then, yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. Best answers are on the pitch."

Sunday's fixture takes place at Atletico Madrid's home, the Metropolitano.

Victory would ensure England win their Nations League group and earn a more favourable quarter-final draw but world champions Spain are unbeaten in 43 matches, including a 3-2 win at Wembley in September.

"It's important that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength," Tuchel added.

"It [Spain] is a team that has forgotten how to lose, so it requires a top performance first of all, and if we can deliver this performance, it will give us a big boost.

"I think we're there, and I think we're ready to win on Sunday,"

item.title: Clough's longevity: landmark achievement or indictment on football?
item.description: Mansfield boss Nigel Clough discusses his longevity and staying power as he becomes a club's longest-serving manager for a second time in his career.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Becoming the longest-serving manager at a club takes some doing in the fickle world of football.

Sticking around at two clubs long enough to hold that mantle is just about unprecedented.

But Mansfield Town's Nigel Clough is about to redefine longevity as a manager when it comes to working at sides that make up the top 92 in the English pyramid.

"I don't think it's particularly an achievement; I think it's more an indictment of football that nobody else has lasted that long," Clough told BBC Sport.

This weekend he becomes the longest-serving manager – in terms of active years in the job and league matches at the helm – of the Stags, where he surpasses club great Ian Greaves.

The 16 years Clough spent at Burton Albion, which took in around 900 matches across two spells spanning more than two decades, means the record at the east Staffordshire side is already his.

Former England forward Clough is now six years and one week into the Stags job and is the second longest-serving manager across England's top four leagues - behind only Mikel Arteta at Arsenal - but he does not see his staying power as anything special.

"I don't really think about it that much, I have to say. I'm just trying to get through the week," said Clough, who has been in charge of Mansfield for 329 matches across all competitions.

When time pays dividends

While Clough's players, as well as Mansfield fans have a different take on what his lengthy tenure at the One Call Stadium has meant, the 60-year-old reeled off the names of legendary past managers - his late father and iconic Nottingham Forest boss Brian Clough included - when reflecting on what joy clubs would have by sticking by their manager.

"When you look back 20 or 30 years, my dad was at Forest for 18 years, Alex Ferguson was at Manchester United for so long and then there was Arsene Wenger at Arsenal. That was at the top level, but even lower down there was a lot of managers who stayed a lot of years," he said

"I just think it's sad the way football is going at the moment. The first bad period that people have, a month, two months or something like that, and the manager is the one that goes."

Clough, who played in the top flight for Forest, Liverpool and Manchester City, has been in management for 28 years and been in charge of just four clubs - Mansfield, Burton, Derby County and Sheffield United - in that time.

Since bounding from non-league level - where he spent the first 10 years of his management career in his first spell at Burton - to take the reins of Derby in the Championship in 2009, no-one has overseen more matches than Clough's 893 across England's top four divisions.

The latest statistics from the League Managers' Association show that managers across those leagues are now staying in their jobs for less than a year on average.

Clough bucking the trend with his record-setting endurance at Mansfield comes in the same week that Manchester United sacked Michael Carrick, when he was 10 months into the job, and Crystal Palace relieved Pierre Sage of his role after only 16 games.

Overcoming 'sticky periods'

When asked if Clough has ever felt his job was under threat during any "sticky period" at Mansfield, he responded with a firm "of course".

It was when the Stags were in the relegation places and on a 12-match winless run in his first full campaign in charge in 2021-22.

He survived that, then oversaw a club-record 11 consecutive home wins and went on to guide Mansfield to the League Two play-off final at Wembley later the same season.

"You've got to go through that period and you've got to get through it," Clough said of dealing with difficult runs as a manager.

"And I think as you get a little bit older, you know more that it's going to change.

"You get a result out of adversity as much as anything. If you're winning, it doesn't keep going, and if you're losing it's the same thing if you've got a reasonable team and you're doing the right things."

What do fans and players think of Clough?

While Mansfield missed out on promotion when they took their bid all the way to the national stadium in 2022, they went up automatically two years later when they finished third in the table.

It ended Mansfield's 21-year absence from the third tier. And when he kept them up in their first season back, Clough did what no-one had done for 35 years.

Last season they finished 10th, the club's highest league placing since 1987 when Greaves guided them to exactly the same position in the standings.

Stags supporter Dean Foulkes says it "has been an incredible journey" at Mansfield since Clough took the helm in November 2020.

The feeling tracks.

At Burton he is a club legend for the way he transformed the Brewers as a non-league side in his first spell there before taking them to the Championship during his second stint.

He leapt a number of divisions when he left Burton the first time to manage Derby - a particularly poignant job as his father took the Rams to their first English title in 1972.

Even at Sheffield United, where Clough had the shortest stint of his managerial career, he guided them to the semi-final of the FA Cup when they were a League One side in 2014.

"He is really good football man to have around. We should be proud that he is Mansfield Town manager," Foulkes told BBC Radio Nottingham.

"Look at what he has achieved, promotion, and we now have players coming to Mansfield Town because they want to play for Nigel Clough."

It is why prolific veteran forward David McGoldrick moved there in the summer, and how the club has enticed former Leeds United forward Tyler Roberts, as well as ex-Preston forward Michael Smith to the Nottinghamshire town while also landing highly-rated Tottenham midfielder George Abbott on loan.

Ryan Sweeney says the chance to play for Clough was "the main reason" he decided to return to the club last summer.

Former Nottingham Forest and Southend striker Stephen McLaughlin says Clough "manages differently to any other manager" he has worked with.

"He doesn't treat you as a number, he treats you as a person and you want to run though bricks walls for him," McLaughlin said.

"It's hard to explain what he does for you on and off the pitch as well. You are not on the grass too long in training because he trusts you to get your work in and to be ready for Saturday.

"He doesn't give too much tactical information to people because the message is 'just do your job and work hard'."

Jordan Bowery has been asked to do that more than most, having been transformed from a striker to a defender and is now seen as 'Mr Versatile'., external

"He is incredibly loyal and trusts me in those positions," Bowery said. "A lot of managers wouldn't do that, but he's had my back and I appreciate that.

"He can get onto you, but that is like most managers. He expects and demands the best out of every single one of you each day.

"He has obviously been around the game a long time, played at the highest level - he knows the game and he knows the players."

'Insight into success' a family business

And Clough, the player, is a former attacker of considerable repute in Nottinghamshire.

No-one has scored more than Clough's 131 goals for Forest over the past 113 years.

It was there, at Mansfield's high-profile county neighbours, where he thrived under his father who famously guided the Reds to the First Division title in 1978 before collecting back-to-back European Cups.

The manager that Clough is has been shaped by the successes he watched up close as a child and those he later revelled in as a player.

"When you're brought up in the household that we were brought up in and the environment we were brought up in, then we have a certain insight into what it takes to have a chance of being successful and what you expect of the team and everything," he said.

"And the empathy, I don't think you should ever forget that if you've been a player as well, how that feels when you have a rough time and so on."

And it is those players, and how they are found before investing in them that is the closest thing to revealing the secret to Clough's longevity.

"We don't like wasting the owners' money," he said.

"Whether it was at Burton when we were in the Dr Martens South [non-league level] or whether it's here at Mansfield Town, we try and look after it as best we can. And we have a responsibility to do that.

"We do as much in-depth research as we can on players. Character is the main feature of what we look at. We can see all the stuff on the videos of what they can do, then we watch them live and everything, but you have to delve really into the character and get a lot of references from players, coaches, managers.

"We take that very seriously. Each season we set out to just try and get a few better players in the squad.

"It's keeping the ball rolling, keeping the owners happy, keeping the supporters happy."

Additional reporting by BBC Radio Nottingham's David Jackson and Jake Garner.

item.title: Japan's unlikely leader who turned down the All Blacks
item.description: Warner Dearns did not want to go to Japan as a teenager. Now he is determined to stay and do his adopted country proud.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Warner Dearns didn't want to go to Japan. Now, he doesn't want to leave.

A decade ago, Dearns' father Grant got a job as a strength and conditioning coach with top-flight Japanese side NEC Green Rockets, taking the family from New Zealand's North Island to a satellite city outside Tokyo.

For Dearns, like most 14-year-olds, swapping class-mates, countries, continents and cultures didn't appeal.

"I said I didn't want to go," says the second row, who will co-captain Japan against England at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.

"My sister and I wanted to stay with our grandma and grandad [in New Zealand]."

But, reluctantly, they made the trip, with Dearns' mother Tanya, a former New Zealand netballer, giving up her own coaching job to help the family settle in Japan.

"The first year or two took a bit to adapt to, it is a very different culture from New Zealand, and the language barrier didn't help much either," remembers Dearns.

"At high school there was no-one else who spoke English. I was the kid who stood out, the only one with blond curly hair, so it was lots of fun."

There were other reasons that Dearns stood out.

Even as a teenager, he stood 6ft 8in tall and weighed more than 19 stone (120.6kg).

In New Zealand, Deans had been more interested in basketball than rugby. But at Kashiwa Senior High School – one of Japan's strongest rugby-playing schools – they moulded him into a monster prospect.

To supplement his size and galloping, long-legged sprint, Dearns' school coaches introduced gymnastics into his training schedule, having him hurdle team-mates and perform flips, to improve his agility around the pitch.

Away from school, he would hit the gym at his dad's employers, working out alongside the likes of former England full-back Alex Goode.

Given that super-charged rugby education, Dearns progressed fast.

Having qualified on residency grounds, he made his Japan debut In November 2021 at just 19.

By France 2023, he was a regular, featuring in all four of the team's matches at the Rugby World Cup.

This past season, he has been a revelation.

He has spent the year back in New Zealand at the Hurricanes on a season's sabbatical, where his bottomless energy, soft hands and line-out prowess helped the Wellington side to their first Super Rugby title in a decade.

Playing alongside All Blacks Jordie Barrett, Ruben Love, Cam Roigard and Peter Lakai, broadened Dearns' horizons once more.

"It was awesome, I got to sit back and see how the boys prepare," Dearns added.

"The All Blacks guys especially lead the way and are part of the leadership group, I got to enjoy playing footy and watch how they do things."

The possibility of Dearns having a more permanent view was raised.

Various figures in New Zealand rugby's scene wondered whether Dearns would be amenable to returning to his homeland, waiting out a three-year Test stand-down requirement and then transferring his allegiance to the All Blacks.

Dearns, now 24, declined.

"It was nothing official, it was all sort of hearsay," he says of the possibility of switching sides.

"I had a couple of people coming up to me asking me if I would ever think about it. It was never an option for me."

Dearns is indebted to Japan for the country's role in his development. But Japan is also now home.

Dearns, who now speaks the language fluently and whose son was born in the country, was moved to tears during his adopted nation's anthem at the last World Cup.

His passion shows in the way he plays too.

On his last visit to Twickenham, back in 2022, Dearns set up a try with a break and offload to scrum-half Naoto Saito. In the teams' most recent meeting, in Tokyo in 2024, he assisted another two, one via a brilliant one-handed grab-and-go in midfield.

On both occasions however, Japan ended up on the wrong end of heavy scorelines.

If they are to shock Twickenham, Dearns will need to marshall an extraordinary forward effort, as well as produce showreel moments.

"It is always a set-piece battle and England do a very good job of scrum and line-out, they are obviously very physical," he says.

Dearns has come a long way. But victory on Saturday would be his biggest step yet.

item.title: Six goals to go - will McGinn catch Dalglish & Law?
item.description: After drawing level with Hughie Gallacher on 24 Scotland goals, will midfielder John McGinn reach Kenny Dalglish and Denis Law's record tally of 30?
item.content:encoded:
• Published

As Scotland legend Kenny Dalglish watched one of his records equalled in Scotland's 2-1 win over North Macedonia, another of his feats loomed into view.

The night was supposed to be about Andy Robertson joining Dalglish as Scotland's most-capped man, the Tottenham left-back making his 102nd appearance for his country.

But instead, for the first time, the 75-year-old might be nervous that his crown as one of Scotland men's all-time top goalscorers is wobbling.

That is because, in Scotland's rather humdrum Nations League victory, John McGinn - in his 94th Scotland appearance - took two big strides towards the record.

The Aston Villa midfielder now has 24 goals for his country - six shy of Dalglish's long-standing record of 30, shared with Denis Law.

"It's something that's been in the back of my head," McGinn admitted in the post-match debrief. "If I start climbing that table, it means we've been successful as a team."

Now 32 years old, time is running out for him. But as he pulls level with Hughie Gallacher, one of the Wembley Wizards of folklore, his ambition is clear.

McGinn 'definitely capable' of reaching record

There was a time when talk of this record being toppled seemed laughable. Scotland has produced strikers in recent decades, but none close to Dalglish or Law.

The fact a midfielder might take the title makes McGinn's feat all the more astonishing.

His prowess in front of goal is no secret to the Tartan Army. There was the spell at the end of 2019 where he scored six in three games, his overhead kick against Austria, his late winner against Croatia in 2024.

But of late, his lack of goals and even his performances have had some fans questioning where he fits into the Scotland team.

"It has been a bit of a dry patch for me over the last year on the goal front," McGinn admitted, and he's not wrong.

He failed to find the back of the net for Scotland in 2025, the first time he'd done that since 2020.

But, just as his form at Villa has sky-rocketed, he came up big for his new international head coach Sebastien Pocognoli.

"Isn't it great to have a John McGinn in your team?" former Scotland winger Pat Nevin said on Sportsound. "He's somebody you'd want to have in your team to be taking a penalty for you.

"I'd be surprised if John McGinn doesn't get the goal record now. It might take him another year or two, but he is definitely capable of getting that record."

'The best person I've met in football'

Becoming Scotland's main penalty taker will help, a fact McGinn alluded to coyly post-match.

In his career, he had only taken one spot-kick before this season - scoring for Scotland in the 3-3 draw against Norway back in 2023.

In this campaign he has scored three and missed one, smacking the bar against Fulham on Halloween.

In classic McGinn fashion, he bounced back to slot home against Manchester United the following week, before being caught on ref-cam admitting to the official that he was nervous to take it after his hitting the woodwork.

That jovial, lovable personality has not just won him fans off the pitch. It is clear that his team-mates at both Villa and the national team adore him.

"He's not going to stop until he [gets the record]," said striker Che Adams, who helped set up McGinn's first against North Macedonia.

"Everyone's pleased for him, he's the best person I've met in football. For him to get the recognition he deserves is amazing."

McGinn's iconic status in Scottish football is secure and will not be tarnished if he fails to climb the mountain.

Whether it is being speared by Steven Thompson in training, calling Scotland performances 'jobby', or admitting he would "probably be at Yeovil" were it not for his backside, the midfielder has already won the heart of a nation.

item.title: England boxer missed Worlds over sex-test mix-up
item.description: George Francis was left “broken” after he was banned from competing at the Under-19 World Championships because his team did not organise a sex verification test to prove he is male.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

A teenage English boxer says he was left "broken" after he was banned from competing at the Under-19 World Championships because his team forgot to organise a sex verification test to prove he is male.

George Francis, 18, was due to fight in the 60kg category in Budva, Montenegro last month.

But he says that he was informed he was ineligible only hours before the draw because of an "administrative oversight" by governing body England Boxing.

"They got me in a room and told me that I couldn't box because they didn't know if I was a boy or a girl, basically," Francis told BBC Sport.

"The explanation was that they couldn't provide a blood sample for me in time. Everyone else was able to provide a blood sample, but they just forgot me.

"Somehow I wasn't on the system. Apparently, there were no qualified doctors in Budva to do it. It's crazy."

A multiple schoolboy and junior national champion, Francis said he had been training "non-stop" for the "dream" of representing England in his first World Championships.

"It was the worst news I've ever had in my life," said the Essex-based fighter, whose plight was first reported by the Times newspaper.

"I wouldn't wish it on anyone, to be honest. I was just broken. They were speaking to me and I couldn't even really hear. I was devastated. I couldn't really talk. I literally couldn't feel anything. There was a hole left there."

World Boxing introduced mandatory genetic sex testing for female competitors aged 18 and above last year to ensure "the safety of all participants and provide a level playing field", with national federations responsible for ensuring samples were processed.

The move followed a major controversy in the women's boxing competition at the 2024 Olympics in Paris, where fighters Imane Khelif and Lin Yu-ting both won golds, despite being disqualified from the previous year's World Championships for allegedly failing sex eligibility tests conducted by the then governing body, the International Boxing Association.

In January however, World Boxing extended the rules to include male boxers.

"I can't put into words how it just doesn't make sense," said Francis, who has now missed out on the chance of trying to qualify for the Olympics, and is planing to turn professional.

"I feel like there's nothing really left for me as an amateur.

"I turned 18 four days before flying, so it must have been that they hadn't checked their system in time to get me tested. Going forward, there should be someone there making sure it doesn't happen because I don't want any of these mistakes happening to anybody else."

While Francis' father has been contacted by Boxing England since the episode, his son claims the governing body is yet to contact him directly.

"I haven't had one phone call or message from them. I've just been forgotten about. I don't know how that's been allowed," he said.

In a statement, England Boxing said it "acknowledges that an administrative oversight occurred, once the issue became apparent, we worked closely with the competition organisers to explore all appropriate options in accordance with World Boxing's rules and regulations.

"We maintained open communication with George and his family throughout, despite this, a resolution was not possible.

"George remained a valued member of the England team, including representing the squad as flag bearer.

"England Boxing has no greater priority than the health and wellbeing of athletes on its performance pathway and are committed to learning from this experience and strengthening our processes to prevent a recurrence."

World Boxing has been approached for comment.

In 2025, a dozen female fighters across five nations were barred from the World Championships in Liverpool because deadlines for their sex tests were missed.

item.title: Warner accuses Cricket Australia of 'cover-up'
item.description: Former vice-captain David Warner accuses Cricket Australia of a "cover-up", claiming Australia's bowlers were not interviewed in ball-tampering investigation.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

David Warner has accused Cricket Australia (CA) of a "cover up" as the row over the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continued.

Former vice-captain Warner, captain Steve Smith and opener Cameron Bancroft all served lengthy bans as part of CA's investigation into the ball-tampering scandal that rocked Australian cricket during a Test series in South Africa in 2018.

Batter Usman Khawaja has reopened discussions about the scandal with explosive claims in his new autobiography, where he said the entire Australia team knew about the use of sandpaper to tamper with the ball.

And Warner has questioned the investigation into the incident by claiming that Australia's bowlers from the Cape Town Test were not interviewed.

"As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said.

"If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?

"It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea.

"That stinks of a cover-up."

The four frontline bowlers - Hazlewood, Starc, Lyon and Pat Cummins - have maintained they did not know about the plan to use sandpaper to tamper with the ball.

Cummins, Australia's Test captain since 2021, said in his extraordinary news conference on Friday that he was interviewed as part of the investigation.

In response to Warner's comments, CA said: "As we have stated previously, all players were given the opportunity to speak at the time of the initial investigation and have had the ability to come forward with new evidence in the eight years since.

"Subsequently, CA has respected every player and former players' right to provide their own version of events."

Warner has been steadfast in his defence of former batting partner and childhood friend Khawaja since his recollections were made public last week.

After Cummins' news conference, in which he said suggestions the entire team knew about the scheme to cheat were "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense", Warner said: "I stick with Uzzie. It's the truth. The captain threw Uzzie under the bus.

"I feel it was a botched investigation."

Khawaja also revealed he was not interviewed as part of the investigation, despite sitting next to Bancroft - the player seen with sandpaper on the field - in the dressing room.

CA has said it will not reopen its investigation.

item.title: The challenge that brought Nunes out of retirement
item.description: Amanda Nunes says the prospect of fighting Kayla Harrison and putting women's MMA back in the spotlight convinced her to come out of retirement to fight at UFC 334 on Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

It was always going to take a special challenge to bring Amanda Nunes out of retirement.

The Brazilian left the UFC in 2023 as the most successful women's mixed martial artist of all time, and with a strong claim to be the greatest ever, regardless of gender.

A former featherweight and bantamweight champion, Nunes is the only woman to hold UFC titles in two weight classes simultaneously, and the only fighter, male or female, to successfully defend both belts.

During Nunes' remarkable run, she beat some of the greatest names in MMA history, such as Ronda Rousey, Cris Cyborg and Valentina Shevchenko.

After Nunes was eventually dethroned by Julianna Pena in one of the biggest upsets of all time, she then regained her title in emphatic fashion.

Nunes was so dominant, she ran out of challengers and left the sport feeling like she had completed MMA.

That was until Kayla Harrison came along.

"When Kayla signed with the UFC and I saw the division with some new girls it excited me," said Nunes.

"Because I cleaned both divisions and didn't have anything to do any more. That was when I was sure I wanted to do this again."

American Harrison is a two-time Olympic gold medallist in judo who became a two-time PFL lightweight world champion after transitioning to MMA.

After joining the UFC in 2024, Harrison won the bantamweight title in only her third fight with the promotion.

The contest between 36-year-old Harrison and 38-year-old Nunes is being described by pundits as one of the biggest women's fights in UFC history.

The pair are friends and former team-mates at American Top Team Gym, before Nunes left in 2022.

They were originally set to fight in January, but the fight got postponed after Harrison required neck and spinal surgery.

They will instead compete at UFC 334 at New York's Madison Square Garden on Saturday.

Nunes beams with excitement at the prospect of returning to the octagon to fight Harrison, and she has lost none of her trademark confidence during her three years away from the sport.

"I'm not here today as a challenger, I'm here today as a double champion," said Nunes.

"I needed a break and did it at the right time for my mind, body and soul.

"There's no hate. It's about the challenge Kayla brings and how great this will be for women's MMA. We want to prove who the best girl is in the cage."

Nunes wants to put women back in spotlight

Nunes has won 23 of her 28 fights since her debut in 2008 during a glittering career, with 13 of those victories coming via knockout.

She holds multiple records, including 11 wins in title fights, which is the most for a woman in UFC history alongside Shevchenko.

Such is Nunes' star power, she has headlined multiple large events during her career, including the landmark UFC 200 show in 2016, where she beat Miesha Tate.

She also headlined when she regained the belt off Pena at UFC 277, and in her last bout against Irene Aldana.

Since then however, only one of 43 UFC numbered events have been headlined by women, which was Natalia Silva's win over Wang Cong at UFC 332 in October.

Nunes says part of her return is fuelled by wanting to help women's MMA return to the spotlight.

"I got upset when I left because I wanted to see the division grow. Back in the day, we put in so much work to this division," said Nunes.

"This is my work here, I want to make women's MMA great, I want the UFC proud of us, so when I saw it slowing down I was a little sad and I got the itch. I want to jump back in and bring it back again."

Nunes has been able to spend more time with her partner Nina and her two daughters during her break from the sport, but admits she has "missed being a fighter".

At the age of 38, it remains to be seen if Nunes' powers have waned, but she says she is planning to fight on past the Harrison match "until my body tells me".

Now, with a new challenge in front of her, Nunes gets the chance to add another chapter to her remarkable story.
